Learning Objectives
Lists indications for extended trochanteric osteotomy.
Explain how to perform an extended trochanteric osteotomy.
Describe the postoperative protocol for extended trochanteric osteotomy.
Identify intraoperative and postoperative complications of extended trochanteric osteotomy.
Review the outcomes of extended trochanteric osteotomy.

Extended trochanteric osteotomy (ETO) is a technique for the safe removal of well-fixed
cementless and cemented femoral components. The technique is associated with many
advantages, including enhanced femoral canal access; prevention of iatrogenic injuries,
such as canal perforation and intraoperative fractures; safe cement removal; enhanced
acetabular exposure; and ability to alter soft-tissue tension.
Indications
Removal of well-fixed uncemented femoral stem.
Removal of cemented femoral stem.
Removal of well-fixed cement mantle.
Need for improved acetabular exposure.
Removal of difficult cement mantle.
Varus remodeling of a proximal femur that prevents appropriate reaming and implantation of
a revision femoral component.
Fractured stem.
Severe trochanteric osteolysis.

Indications
ETO has several indications. Removal of well-fixed uncemented or cemented femoral
stem is the most common indication. It allows for controlled component removal
without causing iatrogenic fracture or considerable bone loss. In a cemented setting,
ETO may ease the removal of a difficult cement mantle by allowing for more thorough
removal under direct visualization.
Another indication for ETO includes a loosened, short femoral stem that causes varus
remodeling of the proximal femur. Varus remodeling may be observed in as many as
30% of loose stems. ETO decreases the risk of subsequent canal perforation, under-
sizing of the revision stem, and placement of the revision stem in varus1 (Figure 1).

Figure 1 AP radiograph of a hip with a cemented total hip arthroplasty implant
demonstrates mechanical failure with associated proximal femoral varus remodeling,
causing a conflict. An extended trochanteric osteotomy is required for correction of the
proximal deformity and distal cement extraction. Note the conflict. (Reproduced from
Sporer SM, Paprosky WG: Revision total hip arthroplasty via extended trochanteric
osteotomy, in Colvin AC, Flatow E, eds: Atlas of Essential Orthopaedic Procedures, ed 2.
Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2000, pp 490-498.)
Additional indications for ETO exist. ETO enables modification of abductor tension by
fixing the fragment in a more proximal or distal position. In patients with severe
trochanteric osteolysis, an ETO can prevent iatrogenic fracture. In addition, ETO can be
used to improve acetabular exposure in patients with heterotopic ossification. In revision

Contraindications
No absolute contraindications
Preoperative Planning
Knowledge of stem type is important (ie, cemented, proximally porous coated, extensively
porous coated).
Using preoperative imaging studies, determine the desired length of the osteotomy, which is
measured from the tip of the greater trochanter.
Osteotomy length based on stem type, stem length, and extent of cement.
In revision procedures for loose stems with varus femoral remodeling, the osteotomy should
reach the apex of the deformity.

Preoperative Planning
In preoperative planning for ETO, knowledge of the type of stem being removed is
necessary. A proximally coated stem generally requires osteotomy only to the distal
extent of the porous coating. Extensively porous-coated stems require planning for a
longer osteotomy. The surgeon also must plan for fixation of the osteotomy fragment
with the use of cables or cable plates.
Patient Positioning
Lateral decubitus position most common.
Also may be performed in the supine position (supine Hardinge).

Patient Positioning

The lateral decubitus position is the most common and preferred position for ETO. For
surgeons most comfortable with the supine Hardinge approach, this position also may
be used.
Surgical Approaches
Posterolateral most common
Most extensile.
Thought to better preserve vascularity of ETO fragment.
A direct lateral approach also may be safely used.
Preserving soft-tissue attachments is important.

Surgical Approaches
In performing an ETO, the posterolateral approach is preferred by most surgeons. The
posterolateral approach is the most extensile, allowing for easy access to the entire
femur, and is thought to best preserve vascularity. ETO also can be performed safely via
a direct lateral approach (Hardinge).
Techniques
The length of the ETO is determined by the length of the implant being revised, the position of
the femoral isthmus, and the extent of cement.
Minimum length of 12 cm suggested.
The borders of the osteotomized fragment include the greater trochanter superiorly, just
lateral to the linea aspera posteriorly, the anterior cortex, and the distal border in the chosen
area of diaphysis.
An oscillating saw is used to make the cut posteriorly.
The distal transverse limb cut is made with the use of a pencil-tipped burr, with rounded
corners to prevent a stress riser.
Osteotomize the distal 1 to 2 cm of the anterior cortex and proximally at the level of the
greater trochanter with the use of an oscillating saw.

The osteotomy should include one-third or less of the circumference of the femoral diaphysis1
(Figure 3).
An uncemented revision stem is recommended.
A prophylactic cable should be placed distally to prevent fracture propagation before
preparing the femur for a revision stem.
Two or three cables for fixation of the osteotomized fragment
Alternatively, cable plate fixation in compromised bone or fractured osteotomy fragment
Figure 3 Illustrations show the location of an extended trochanteric osteotomy on the anterior
(A) and posterior (B) aspects of the femur. The length of the osteotomy is measured from the tip
of the greater trochanter. Depending on the indication for the osteotomy, the trochanteric
fragment should allow for placement of a minimum of two cerclage wires and generally should
be at least 15 to 16 cm long. (Reproduced from Sporer SM, Paprosky WG: Revision total hip
arthroplasty via extended trochanteric osteotomy, in Colvin AC, Flatow E, eds: Atlas of Essential

Orthopaedic Procedures ed 2. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020,


Techniques
In performing an ETO, the posterior border of the linea aspera is first exposed by
elevating the vastus lateralis. The predetermined length of the osteotomy should be
marked with the use of a pen or electrocautery. A thin saw blade should be used to cut
the posterior limb from proximal at the level of the greater trochanter to distal. A high-
speed pencil-tipped burr can be used for the distal, transverse cut to round the corners
carefully, avoiding creation of a stress riser and, therefore, fracture propagation. The
transverse cut should include one-third or less of the diaphyseal circumference. The
anterior limb cut should be made proximally and distally with the use of a thin saw
blade. Broad osteotomes are then inserted and stacked under the posterior limb as the
fragment is lifted anteriorly. After completed, a prophylactic cable is recommended just
distal to the osteotomy to prevent propagation. After stem insertion, two or three cables
should be used for fixation of the osteotomized fragment. A cable plate also may be
used in patients with poor bone stock or a fractured osteotomy fragment (Video 1).

Postoperative Management
Toe-touch weight bearing for 6 weeks followed by advancement to partial–weight bearing is
recommended.
Advance to full–weight bearing at 12 weeks postoperatively.
No active abduction or straight leg raises are allowed for 12 weeks postoperatively or until
radiographic union is observed. This reduces stress on the osteotomy repair.
Consider a hip abduction brace.

Postoperative Management
Although the postoperative protocol for ETO varies, most surgeons advocate for toe-
touch weight bearing for 6 weeks postoperatively followed by 6 weeks of partial–weight
bearing. Full–weight bearing is permitted at 12 weeks postoperatively. Active abduction
and straight leg raises are prohibited until 12 weeks postoperatively. Some surgeons
progress activity based on radiographic healing.
Pitfalls and Preventive Measures
Complications
Fracture of osteotomy fragment most common.
Migration of osteotomized fragment.
Nonunion.
Fixation failure.
Dislocation.
Neurovascular injury.


Complications
The most common complication of ETO is fracture of the osteotomized fragment.
Nonunion, malunion, and migration of the osteotomized fragment also are well-known
complications that can be mitigated by proper fixation. Failed fixation (ie, cable
loosening) may occur. Dislocation because of alteration in abductor tension has been
described; however, most dislocations are not specifically related to the osteotomy.
Neurovascular injury has been reported, most likely during placement of a cable or wire.
Outcomes
Substantially higher rate of iatrogenic fracture without ETO.
Survival rate after ETO greater than 90%.
Nonunion rate after ETO very low in septic and aseptic cases (zero to 5%).
In two-stage revision, metallic fixation may be used to repair the osteotomized fragment
during the first stage without hindering infection eradication and, therefore, the success of the
second stage.
ETO fixation with the use of cables is superior to cerclage wires.
ETO reduces torsional strength of the femur, even after femoral stem insertion and osteotomy
repair.

Outcomes
Outcomes of ETO are excellent. A substantially higher rate of iatrogenic fracture has
been reported without ETO. The nonunion rate after ETO is very low (zero to 5%). A
greater than 90% survival rate is associated with aseptic revision in which ETO is
performed. In septic cases, ETO may be performed to remove the stem during two-stage
revision, with excellent union rates and no increase in re-infection with the use of
metallic fixation in the first stage. Conversely, ETO reduces the torsional strength of the
femur, even after femoral stem insertion and osteotomy repair.
